message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


YOUR DIMENSION: is_ascii_domain (line 3) and is_idn_domain (line 4).
Determine precisely:
- Is is_ascii_domain simply "every byte <= 0x7F"? Sweep bytes: for each of 0x01..0x7F confirm ascii=1; for each of 0x80..0xFF (as a raw lone byte via printf '\xNN', which is INVALID UTF-8) confirm ascii=0. Report any byte that breaks the pattern.
- Is is_idn_domain exactly the negation of is_ascii_domain for NON-EMPTY input? Find any input where line3 and line4 are BOTH 1, or BOTH 0 (empty string gives 1 and 0 — confirm and note it).
- Empty input: confirm ascii=1, idn=0.
- Does is_idn_domain do anything with the "xn--" ACE prefix? Test "xn--fsq.com", "XN--FSQ.COM", "xn--", "xn--a", "bare-xn--inside". Establish whether punycode prefixes affect line 4 at all.
- Does validity of UTF-8 matter? Test lone continuation bytes (0x80-0xBF), truncated sequences (0xC3 alone, 0xE4 0xBE alone), overlong encodings (0xC0 0x80), and 0xFE/0xFF.
- Interaction with length: is a >255-byte non-ASCII string still ascii=0 / idn=1? Confirm lines 3/4 are independent of the validity lines.

cd /workspace/dataset
echo "=== fuzz: 4000 random byte strings, check line3 XOR line4 and ascii==(no byte>=0x80) ==="
viol_xor=0; viol_pred=0; n=0; both1=0; both0=0
for i in $(seq 1 4000); do
  len=$(( (RANDOM % 12) + 1 ))
  s=$(head -c $((len*4)) /dev/urandom | tr -d '\000' | head -c $len)
  [ -z "$s" ] && continue
  n=$((n+1))
  out=$(./test4_executable "$s")
  l3=$(echo "$out" | sed -n 3p); l4=$(echo "$out" | sed -n 4p)
  # predicted ascii: 1 if no byte >= 0x80
  if printf '%s' "$s" | LC_ALL=C grep -qP '[\x80-\xff]' 2>/dev/null; then pred=0; else pred=1; fi
  [ "$l3" = "$l4" ] && { if [ "$l3" = 1 ]; then both1=$((both1+1)); else both0=$((both0+1)); fi; viol_xor=$((viol_xor+1)); printf 'XORVIOL l3=%s l4=%s hex=%s\n' "$l3" "$l4" "$(printf '%s' "$s" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')"; }
  [ "$l3" != "$pred" ] && { viol_pred=$((viol_pred+1)); printf 'PREDVIOL l3=%s pred=%s hex=%s\n' "$l3" "$pred" "$(printf '%s' "$s" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')"; }
done
echo "tested=$n xor_violations=$viol_xor (both1=$both1 both0=$both0) pred_violations=$viol_pred"

input.command:
cd /workspace/dataset
echo "=== fuzz v2: od-based predicate, 3000 random strings ==="
viol_xor=0; viol_pred=0; n=0
for i in $(seq 1 3000); do
  len=$(( (RANDOM % 16) + 1 ))
  s=$(head -c $((len*4)) /dev/urandom | tr -d '\000\012' | head -c $len)
  [ -z "$s" ] && continue
  n=$((n+1))
  out=$(./test4_executable "$s")
  l3=$(echo "$out" | sed -n 3p); l4=$(echo "$out" | sed -n 4p)
  hex=$(printf '%s' "$s" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
  # pred=0 if any byte value >= 0x80 (first hex nibble in 8..f)
  pred=$(printf '%s' "$hex" | awk '{r=1; for(i=1;i<=length($0);i+=2){b=substr($0,i,2); if (b ~ /^[89abcdef]/) {r=0}} print r}')
  if [ "$l3" = "$l4" ]; then viol_xor=$((viol_xor+1)); echo "XORVIOL l3=$l3 l4=$l4 hex=$hex"; fi

content.text: All confirmed with zero violations across ~11,000 test cases. Writing up findings.

rules.statement: is_ascii_domain(s) == 1 if and only if every byte of s has value <= 0x7F (i.e. no byte has the high bit set). It is a pure per-byte high-bit test — no structural, length, UTF-8, or label parsing is involved.
rules.evidence:
Exhaustive lone-byte sweep over all 255 representable byte values (0x00 cannot be passed via argv):

  cd /workspace/dataset
  for i in $(seq 1 255); do h=$(printf '%02x' $i);
    if [ "$h" = "0a" ]; then out=$(./test4_executable $'\x0a' | tr -d '\n');
    else out=$(./test4_executable "$(printf "\\x$h")" | tr -d '\n'); fi
    echo "$h $out"; done > /tmp/all.txt
  awk '{print substr($2,3,2)}' /tmp/all.txt | sort | uniq -c

Output:
    128 01
    127 10

line3=1 for exactly these 127 bytes: 01 02 ... 7e 7f
line3=0 for exactly these 128 bytes: 80 81 ... fe ff

(NOTE: a naive loop using $(printf '\x0a') silently yields the EMPTY string because command substitution strips trailing newlines; 0x0a must be passed as $'\x0a'. With that fix, lone 0x0a -> 1110, i.e. ascii=1.)

Same partition holds when the byte is embedded in an otherwise-valid domain:
  for i in $(seq 1 255); do h=$(printf '%02x' $i); echo "$h $(./test4_executable "$(printf "a\\x${h}b.com")" | tr -d '\n')"; done
  -> bytes 01..7f all give 1110 (127 cases, no exceptions)
  -> bytes 80..ff all give 1101 (128 cases, no exceptions)

rules.statement: The 0x7F/0x80 boundary is exact: 0x7D, 0x7E, 0x7F give ascii=1/idn=0 and 0x80, 0x81, 0x82 give ascii=0/idn=1, in lone, embedded, and whole-label positions.
rules.evidence:
cd /workspace/dataset
for h in 7d 7e 7f 80 81 82; do
  a=$(./test4_executable "$(printf "\\x$h")" | tr -d '\n')
  b=$(./test4_executable "$(printf "a\\x${h}b.com")" | tr -d '\n')
  c=$(./test4_executable "$(printf "\\x$h.com")" | tr -d '\n')
  printf '0x%s  lone=%s  embedded=%s  label=%s\n' "$h" "$a" "$b" "$c"; done

Output:
0x7d  lone=1110  embedded=1110  label=1110
0x7e  lone=1110  embedded=1110  label=1110
0x7f  lone=1110  embedded=1110  label=1110
0x80  lone=1101  embedded=1101  label=1101
0x81  lone=1101  embedded=1101  label=1101
0x82  lone=1101  embedded=1101  label=1101

rules.statement: is_idn_domain(s) is the exact logical complement of is_ascii_domain(s) for ALL inputs, including the empty string. line3 XOR line4 == 1 always; there is no input where both are 1 or both are 0. Equivalently: is_idn_domain(s) == 1 iff at least one byte of s is >= 0x80.
rules.evidence:
Randomized differential search for a XOR violation — three independent fuzz campaigns, 8498 total cases, ZERO violations.

(1) 3998 random raw-byte strings (len 1..12) from /dev/urandom: xor_violations=0 (both1=0 both0=0)

(2) 3000 random raw-byte strings (len 1..16) with an od-based reference predicate:
  for i in $(seq 1 3000); do len=$(( (RANDOM % 16) + 1 ))
    s=$(head -c $((len*4)) /dev/urandom | tr -d '\000\012' | head -c $len); [ -z "$s" ] && continue
    out=$(./test4_executable "$s"); l3=$(echo "$out"|sed -n 3p); l4=$(echo "$out"|sed -n 4p)
    hex=$(printf '%s' "$s" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n')
    pred=$(printf '%s' "$hex" | awk '{r=1; for(k=1;k<=length($0);k+=2){b=substr($0,k,2); if (b ~ /^[89abcdef]/) r=0} print r}')
    [ "$l3" = "$l4" ] && echo "XORVIOL ..."; [ "$l3" != "$pred" ] && echo "PREDVIOL ..."; done
  Output: RESULT tested=3000 xor_violations=0 pred_violations=0

(3) 1500 domain-shaped strings built from alphabet {a b z 0 9 - _ . * / space A Z ~ ! xn--} plus UTF-8 chars {例 é 😀 ñ ü 中 Ω א}:
  Output: RESULT tested=1500 xor_violations=0 pred_violations=0

Partitioned confirmation (2400 more cases):
  1200 random PURE-ASCII strings (bytes 0x01-0x7F, len 1..40) -> pure-ascii violations=0 (all gave l3l4 = "10")
  1200 random strings with a guaranteed >=1 high byte injected at a random position -> high-byte violations=0 (all gave l3l4 = "01")

Exhaustive lone-byte sweep also shows only two (line3,line4) pairs exist: "10" (127x) and "01" (128x). Never "11", never "00".

rules.statement: Empty input gives ascii=1, idn=0 — but this is NOT a special case; it falls out naturally from the byte predicate (an empty string contains no byte >= 0x80, so it is trivially all-ASCII and trivially contains no non-ASCII). Note this contrasts with lines 1/2, where empty gives 0/0.
rules.evidence:
/workspace/dataset/test4_executable "" -> 0 0 1 0   (line3=1, line4=0)

Strings that are non-empty but structurally degenerate behave identically on lines 3/4:
  for s in "." ".." "..." "...."; do printf '%-6s %s\n' "$s" "$(./test4_executable "$s" | tr -d '\n')"; done
.      1110
..     1110
...    1110
....   1110

So empty and all-dots agree on lines 3/4 (ascii=1, idn=0) while differing on lines 1/2.

rules.statement: The "xn--" ACE / punycode prefix has ZERO effect on line 4 (and on line 3). is_idn_domain does not detect A-labels; a fully-ASCII punycoded IDN such as "xn--fsq.com" reports idn=0. Case of the prefix is likewise irrelevant.
rules.evidence:
cd /workspace/dataset
for s in "xn--fsq.com" "XN--FSQ.COM" "xn--" "xn--a" "bare-xn--inside" "Xn--fsq.com" "xN--fsq.com" "xn--fsq" "a.xn--fsq.b" "xn" "xn-" "xn---" "--xn--"; do printf '%-18s %s\n' "$s" "$(./test4_executable "$s" | tr -d '\n')"; done

Output (every single one is 1110, i.e. ascii=1 idn=0):
xn--fsq.com        1110
XN--FSQ.COM        1110
xn--               1110
xn--a              1110
bare-xn--inside    1110
Xn--fsq.com        1110
xN--fsq.com        1110
xn--fsq            1110
a.xn--fsq.b        1110
xn                 1110
xn-                1110
xn---              1110
--xn--             1110

And "xn--" combined with a high byte just follows the byte rule:
  ./test4_executable "xn--$(printf '\xff')"        -> 1101 (ascii=0, idn=1)
  ./test4_executable "$(printf '\xe4\xbe\x8b')xn--.com" -> 1101
  ./test4_executable "xn--例子.com"                -> 1101
Note "xn--fsq.com" (ASCII form of 例.com) gives idn=0 while "例子.测试" gives idn=1 — proof that line 4 keys on raw bytes, not on IDN semantics.

rules.statement: UTF-8 well-formedness is completely irrelevant to lines 3/4. Lone continuation bytes, truncated sequences, overlong encodings, surrogate encodings, out-of-range encodings, and the never-valid bytes 0xFE/0xFF all behave identically to well-formed multi-byte UTF-8: ascii=0, idn=1.
rules.evidence:

t "$(printf '\x80')" "lone cont 0x80"                    -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xbf')" "lone cont 0xBF"                    -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc3')" "truncated 0xC3 alone"              -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc3\xa9')" "valid 2-byte e-acute"          -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xe4\xbe')" "truncated 0xE4 0xBE"           -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xe4\xbe\x8b')" "valid 3-byte U+4F8B"       -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc0\x80')" "overlong 0xC0 0x80"            -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xc1\xbf')" "overlong 0xC1 0xBF"            -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xfe')" "0xFE"                              -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xff')" "0xFF"                              -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xfe\xff')" "0xFE 0xFF"                     -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xed\xa0\x80')" "UTF-16 surrogate D800"     -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xf4\x90\x80\x80')" "above U+10FFFF"        -> 1101
t "$(printf '\xf0\x9f\x98\x80')" "valid 4-byte emoji"    -> 1101

All 18 cases identical: ascii=0, idn=1. Also all 128 bytes 0x80..0xFF, both lone and embedded, give 1101 with no exceptions (see rule 1 evidence).

rules.statement: Lines 3/4 are completely independent of lines 1/2 (length limits and validity). A single high byte flips lines 3/4 at any length and any position, including inputs that fail both the 63-byte label limit and the 255-byte domain limit. All six reachable 4-line combinations 1110, 1010, 0010, 1101, 1001, 0001 were observed.
rules.evidence:
cd /workspace/dataset
rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }

ASCII, varying length (lines 3/4 pinned at 1/0 while lines 1/2 flip):
  a x63   -> 1110 | a x64  -> 1010 | a x254 -> 1010 | a x255 -> 1010
  a x256  -> 0010 | a x300 -> 0010 | a x1000 -> 0010

Non-ASCII, varying length (lines 3/4 pinned at 0/1 while lines 1/2 flip):
  例 x21 (63B)  -> 1101
  例 x84 (252B) -> 1001
  例 x85 (255B) -> 1001
  例 x86 (258B) -> 0001    <- >255 bytes AND non-ASCII: still ascii=0 / idn=1
  例 x100 (300B) -> 0001
  例 x400 (1200B) -> 0001

One high byte appended/prepended to an over-limit ASCII string still flips 3/4:
  "$(rep 255 a)$(printf '\xff')"  (256B) -> 0001
  "$(rep 1000 a)$(printf '\xff')" (1001B) -> 0001
  "$(printf '\xff')$(rep 1000 a)" (1001B) -> 0001

Position independence (U+00E9 = 0xC3 0xA9 inserted at index 0,1,31,62,63 of a 63-char ASCII string): all -> 1001

No cap even at 100 KB:
  s=$(head -c 100000 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
  ./test4_executable "$s"                        -> 0010
  ./test4_executable "$s$(printf '\xff')"        -> 0001
  ./test4_executable "$(printf '\xff')$s"        -> 0001
  s4=$(head -c 100002 /dev/zero | tr '\0' $'\xc3'); ./test4_executable "$s4" -> 0001

rules.statement: is_ascii_domain does NOT restrict to LDH (letters/digits/hyphen) or any domain-legal character set. Control characters (0x01-0x1F, 0x7F), space, and every printable ASCII symbol including '*', '/', '_', ' ', '~', '!', '\\' all count as ASCII and yield ascii=1.
rules.evidence:
From the exhaustive lone-byte sweep, line3=1 for the complete contiguous run 01..7f with no gaps:
  awk '{print substr($2,3,1), $1}' /tmp/all.txt | awk '$1==1{printf "%s ",$2}END{print ""}'
  01 02 03 ... 1f 20 21 22 ... 2f 30 ... 5f 60 ... 7e 7f   (127 values, contiguous)

Also confirmed embedded: every byte 0x01-0x7F in "a\xNNb.com" -> 1110 (127/127).
And a 300-byte string of only 0x7F (DEL):
  s=$(for ((i=0;i<300;i++)); do printf '\x7f'; done); ./test4_executable "$s" -> 0010  (ascii=1, idn=0; lines 1/2 fail only on length)

openQuestions: Cannot distinguish, black-box, between `is_idn_domain(s) == !is_ascii_domain(s)` and `is_idn_domain(s) == any_of(s, byte >= 0x80)`. The two formulations are extensionally identical on every possible input, including the empty string (empty contains no high byte, so both give idn=0). An implementer may pick either; they will agree on all tests.
Likewise cannot detect whether is_idn_domain contains an explicit `if (s.empty()) return false;` guard, because the empty string is pure ASCII anyway and would return 0 through either path.

The NUL byte 0x00 is untestable through this harness (argv strings are NUL-terminated), so behavior on embedded NUL is unknown. If the implementation is byte-length-based rather than strlen-based this could matter, but it cannot be probed with `test4_executable "<domain-string>"`.

Cannot distinguish the likely implementations `(unsigned char)c < 0x80`, `(signed char)c >= 0`, `c <= 0x7F`, or `!(c & 0x80)` — all four produce the observed exhaustive 0x01-0x7F / 0x80-0xFF partition.

Not probed: whether the two functions short-circuit on the first offending byte or scan the whole string. This is unobservable from output; only extreme-length timing could hint at it, and 100 KB inputs returned instantly in both directions.
